title: Identity Resolution

toc.text: Exercise 1: Match the rules to the scenarios

html:
Identity resolution is the process that turns many rows about the "same" customer into one Unified Individual. It is one of the highest-weighted and most-misunderstood areas of the exam. This phase covers matching rules, reconciliation rules, rulesets, exact vs fuzzy matching, unified profiles, and the operational art of tuning over- and under-merging.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this phase, you will be able to:

  • Explain why identity resolution matters and what a Unified Individual is.
  • Distinguish deterministic (exact) matching from probabilistic (fuzzy) matching.
  • Configure matching rules, reconciliation rules, and identity resolution rulesets.
  • Predict the effect of rule order, confidence thresholds, and key quality on profile quality.
  • Use the lab's IdentityResolutionHelperService (with Identity_Resolution_Candidate__c) to demonstrate scoring.

1. The Problem

A real customer contacts you via web (email a@x.com), phone (number +1555...), loyalty (id LOY-12), and a retailer POS (customer_id 9001). Before identity resolution, Data 360 holds four separate rows pointing at one human. After resolution, they all link to one Unified Individual — a 360° view.

text
Before:   POS cust 9001 | CRM contact | loyalty LOY-12 | web session
After:    UnifiedIndividual  IND-0001
              ├── Individual (CRM contact)     ties: sfdc_recordId, email, phone
              ├── Individual (POS customer)    ties: cust_id, phone
              ├── LoyaltyProfile               tie: LOY-12
              └── Events (web)                 tie: email

The output object is the UnifiedIndividual DMO (UnifiedIndividual__dlm), and it is what segments, activations, and agents consume.

2. Exact vs Fuzzy Matching

Two families of matching operate on matching fields (email, phone, name+address, external id):

Deterministic (exact)Probabilistic (fuzzy)
Match basisValue must be identicalSimilarity/heuristic (name+address proximity)
ConfidenceHigh, low false-positiveMedium, higher recall
UseThe "same key" case: email, loyalty id, external idUgly data: "Rob" vs "Robert", address typos
RiskUnder-merging if keys are missingOver-merging if thresholds are loose

Both rules produce a confidence score. Matching rules have a confidence threshold that must be met (or exceeded) for two records to be declared a match.

Rule anatomy

A matching rule needs:

  1. Matching fields — which DMO fields to compare (ContactPointEmail.email, Individual.fullName, ContactPointPhone.phone).
  2. Match type — exact or fuzzy.
  3. Confidence threshold — minimum score to accept.
  4. (Fuzzy) distance algorithm + accepted range — e.g. name similarity within a Levenshtein range.

Reconciliation rules

When two records match but conflict (two different emails, two names), reconciliation rules decide whose value wins for the unified profile. E.g. CRM overrides POS, most-recent update wins, or merge/canonical values. Getting reconciliation wrong yields a unified profile that displays the wrong phone — the classic "consultant defeated by their own data" bug.

3. Rulesets and the Resolution Run

A ruleset is an ordered group of matching rules + reconciliation rules that Data 360 runs as one identity-resolution job.

  1. Create the ruleset and order the rules (generally: strictest/high-confidence rules first, fuzzy later).
  2. Assign DML (delta/merge) policy — what merges promote into the Unified profile.
  3. Run the ruleset (full run or incremental). The job scores record pairs, applies thresholds, and merges.
  4. Review the output with Profile Explorer: inspect unified profiles, per-source record ties, and rules that fired.

Rule-order intuition

  • Rules are evaluated in order; a stop-on-match design can prevent weird late fuzzy merges.
  • Exact-email first, then exact-phone, then email+fuzzy-name, then fuzzy name+address last.
  • Wide fuzzy rules after targeted exact rules preserve precision while gaining recall.

4. Tuning: Over-merge vs Under-merge

Operational identity work is dominated by tuning. Use the symptom table:

SymptomDirectionFix
Unified profiles contain two different peopleover-mergeraise the fuzzy confidence threshold; restrict fuzzy fields; add a strong reconciliation rule; break entries
Same person appears in 2+ unified profilesunder-mergeadd an exact rule on a key field; add a fuzzy rule; relax threshold; ensure key fields are populated in mapping
Profile loses the latest email/phonereconciliation issueset the correct source priority in reconciliation rules
Big city name+address collides (Apartment buildings)over-mergeuse postcode+street rather than city; keep fuzzy on name only

Data quality work upstream (dedupe at ingestion, pick the right PKs) makes identity resolution dramatically easier — consultants always check the DLO/DMO mapping before blaming the ruleset.

5. The Lab: IdentityResolutionHelperService

Since a ruleset cannot be source-controlled, the lab model implements the scoring logic in Apex:

apex
public with sharing class IdentityResolutionHelperService {

    public static final Integer EXACT_SCORE = 100;
    public static final Integer NO_MATCH   = 0;

    // Score two candidate rows on the same matching field.
    public static Integer scoreExact(String left, String right) {
        if (left == null || right == null) return NO_MATCH;
        return left.equalsIgnoreCase(right) ? EXACT_SCORE : NO_MATCH;
    }

    public static Decimal levenshtein(String a, String b) { /* fuzzy distance 0..1 */ }

    // returns true when score >= threshold (boundary-guarded)
    public static Boolean passesThreshold(Decimal score, Decimal threshold) {
        return score != null && threshold != null && score >= Math.min(threshold, 100);
    }
}

Its test class asserts exact scoring, the fuzzy distance range [0,1], threshold boundary behavior (score == threshold passes), and null-safety. This mirrors the mental model for any matching rule you configure in the real product (threshold inclusive, fields normalized, nulls never match).

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 1: Match the rules to the scenarios

  1. "Two rows where email is identical" → ?
  2. "Two rows where name is Rob vs Robert and address matches" → ?
  3. "Two rows where loyalty id matches but name differs" → ?

Use the table: exact email / exact loyalty id / fuzzy name+address.

Exercise 2: Score by hand

Given thresholds — email exact = 100 (thresh 90), phone exact = 100 (thresh 90), fuzzy name+address min 70 — decide matches for these pairs: (a) same email, (b) same phone + same name, (c) "Rob Smith/10 Main St" vs "Robert Smyth/10 Main St" at fuzzy score 78, (d) same name only. State which are matches and which need rule additions.

Exercise 3: Tune the lab service

Add a scoreFuzzy call path and a new test asserting levenshtein('a@x.com','a@x.com') is exact and levenshtein('abc','xyz') is below any reasonable threshold. Then simulate an over-merge: raise the threshold in a test to show a borderline pair now fails (passesThreshold boundary test exists as an anchor).

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
Identity resolutionThe process of linking multiple records for the same individual/account into a unified profile.
Unified IndividualThe resolved person profile (UnifiedIndividual DMO) after resolution.
Matching ruleConfig that compares matching fields and produces a confidence score.
Exact / deterministicMatch when values are identical (high precision).
Fuzzy / probabilisticSimilarity-based match (higher recall, tuned by threshold).
Confidence thresholdMinimum score required to declare a match.
Reconciliation ruleDecides which conflicting value wins in the unified profile.
RulesetOrdered set of matching + reconciliation rules executed as a job.
Over-merge / under-mergeTwo failure modes: merged different people / failed to merge the same person.
Profile ExplorerThe UI to inspect unified profiles and per-source ties.

Certification Checkpoints

  • I can explain what a Unified Individual is and which ruleset elements create it.
  • I can choose exact vs fuzzy matching and set a threshold for a scenario.
  • I can apply reconciliation rules to fix conflicting profile values.
  • I can diagnose and tune over-merge vs under-merge using Profile Explorer.
  • I can extend and test IdentityResolutionHelperService.

Self-Check

  1. Q: A consultant reports that two distinct customers now appear in one unified profile after a fuzzy rule was added. What is the most likely change to make? — A: Raise the fuzzy rule's confidence threshold (or restrict its matching fields) to reduce over-merge.
  2. Q: Why does calling scoreExact(null, 'x@y.com') return 0? — A: Identity data with missing matching fields must never produce a false match; the lab scores nulls as no-match (same behaviour as a well-configured ruleset).
  3. Q: Where would you inspect which specifically rules fired for a bad profile? — A: Profile Explorer / the resolution run's review UI, which lists rule-level ties per profile.
